title: Ancestral Sesame Transformation, Narrative Resilience, and Neuroprotection in Women Survivors of the Colombian Armed Conflict: An Integrative Narrative and Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Study
content: Armed conflict generates long-term effects on mental health, social cohesion, and community resilience. In post-conflict settings, ancestral food practices may represent important yet underexplored mechanisms for preserving identity, promoting well-being, and facilitating recovery. This study explored the relationships between artisanal sesame (Sesamum indicum L.) transformation, resilience, and health perceptions among women survivors of the Colombian armed conflict in the Montes de María region. Ten women involved in the traditional production of sesame paste participated in a qualitative narrative study. Oral narratives were analyzed using a five-stage interpretative framework comprising transcription and coding, textual analysis, contextual analysis, metatextual reconfiguration, and artificial intelligence-assisted sentiment analysis using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC-22). The narratives revealed five major themes: intergenerational transmission of ancestral knowledge, embodied technical expertise, economic sustainability, cultural identity, and perceived health benefits. Participants consistently described sesame transformation as a source of livelihood, dignity, family continuity, and community cohesion. LIWC-22 analysis demonstrated high social orientation, elevated cognitive processing, strong authenticity, and limited predominance of negative emotional language despite histories of displacement and violence. These findings suggest that artisanal sesame transformation functions as a multidimensional resilience practice linking collective memory, cultural continuity, emotional recovery, and food sovereignty. We propose an “Ancestral Food-Based Neuroresilience” framework integrating traditional food systems, psychosocial adaptation, and health promotion in post-conflict communities.
